1. Core Clinical Tension: A 73-year-old male with a history of coronary artery bypass grafting and mitral valve replacement presented with acute fever, hemoptysis, and rapidly decompensated into septic shock and severe hypoxemic respiratory failure (PaO2/FiO2 ~81). The presence of bilateral lung infiltrates, acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, elevated pro-BNP, atrial fibrillation, and CTPA evidence of pulmonary branch emboli created profound clinical diagnostic tension between fulminant bacterial community-acquired pneumonia, acute pulmonary embolism with infarction, cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and an environmental zoonosis with pulmonary hemorrhage.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs following emergency department triage, intubation and mechanical ventilation, initial ICU physical examination, arterial blood gas analysis, complete blood counts, hepatic/renal panels, cardiac echocardiography, and admission chest CT/CTPA, immediately prior to comprehensive microbiological/serological testing, bedside bronchoscopy, and bronchoalveolar lavage mNGS/fungal cultures.
3. Differential Distinctions: Severe bacterial community-acquired pneumonia was initially suspected and managed with piperacillin/tazobactam followed by imipenem/cilastatin and vancomycin, but the patient deteriorated and all bacterial, viral, and routine fungal cultures and stains were negative. Acute pulmonary embolism and cardiogenic shock were considered given CTPA branch emboli, elevated pro-BNP, and reduced ejection fraction (45%), but venous duplex was negative for deep vein thrombosis and therapy for heart failure failed to halt the pulmonary hemorrhage. Pulmonary hemorrhagic leptospirosis complicated by invasive pulmonary aspergillosis was definitively established when bronchoalveolar lavage mNGS identified Leptospira interrogans and Aspergillus flavus (confirmed on culture), with subsequent clinical resolution on targeted penicillin G and voriconazole.
case_prompt:
A 73-year-old male presented to the emergency department with a 4-day history of fever, general malaise, and hemoptysis. His medical history was notable for coronary artery disease and valvular heart disease, for which he had undergone coronary artery bypass grafting and mitral valve replacement seven years prior; he had recovered well post-operatively and was maintained on oral enteric-coated aspirin and atorvastatin calcium. Four days prior to presentation, he developed fever without an obvious inciting event, peaking at 38.3 °C, accompanied by mild hemoptysis, general fatigue, and chest tightness. Shortly after arrival in the emergency department, his clinical condition acutely deteriorated with impaired consciousness, shock, and profound hypoxemic respiratory failure, necessitating emergency endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation before admission to the intensive care unit.

On physical examination in the intensive care unit, his body temperature was 36.3 °C (after antipyretic administration), pulse rate was 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 16 breaths per minute on the ventilator, and blood pressure was 165/115 mmHg while receiving continuous intravenous norepinephrine at 0.27 mcg/kg/min. He was sedated and mechanically ventilated. Bilateral pupil diameters were 2.0 mm with absent light reflexes. Auscultation of the chest revealed coarse breath sounds and audible bilateral moist rales. Cardiac examination revealed an irregular rhythm consistent with atrial fibrillation without audible murmurs. The abdomen was soft, flat, and non-tender. Mild bilateral lower-extremity edema was noted, and Babinski signs were negative bilaterally.

Arterial blood gas analysis on admission demonstrated severe type I respiratory failure with an oxygenation index (PaO2/FiO2 ratio) of 80.9. Admission laboratory testing demonstrated significant systemic inflammation, with marked elevations in neutrophils, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin. Complete blood count showed a white blood cell count of 14.03 x 10^9/L, hemoglobin of 100 g/L, and platelet count of 48 x 10^9/L. Serum biochemistry demonstrated acute kidney injury with a creatinine of 285 umol/L, mildly elevated transaminases and direct bilirubin, and a markedly elevated pro-brain natriuretic peptide (pro-BNP). Bedside electrocardiography confirmed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 114 beats per minute. Transthoracic echocardiography showed decreased left ventricular systolic function, right ventricular enlargement, and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 45%. Lower extremity Doppler ultrasonography was negative for deep vein thrombosis. Emergency thoracic computed tomography (CT) on admission demonstrated diffuse exudative lesions throughout both lungs; CT pulmonary angiography revealed multiple branch embolisms in the pulmonary arteries of both lungs.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Fulminant onset of fever, respiratory failure, high procalcitonin, and bilateral consolidations suggested severe bacterial pneumonia; however, the patient deteriorated despite broad-spectrum empiric coverage, and comprehensive conventional microbiologic stains, cultures, and serologies were completely negative.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: To detect the etiology of the pneumonia, we performed a series of microbiologic diagnostics including staining and culture and serologic testing for viruses, bacteria, and fungi, all of which were negative (Table 2)... After the patient was transferred to the ICU, due to the consideration of severe community-acquired pneumonia, the condition progressed rapidly, and the initial anti infection treatment failed.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Acute Pulmonary Thromboembolism / Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: History of cardiac surgery, atrial fibrillation, elevated pro-BNP, reduced ejection fraction, and CT pulmonary angiography showing multiple pulmonary artery branch embolisms suggested acute thromboembolism and hydrostatic edema; however, lower extremity Doppler showed no deep vein thrombosis, and bronchoscopy subsequently revealed active diffuse bronchial mucosal hemorrhage rather than simple transudate.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: CT pulmonary angiography revealed multiple pulmonary artery branch embolisms in both lungs (Figure 2). Color Doppler ultrasound of the heart showed decreased left ventricular systolic function, enlarged right heart, and a cardiac ejection fraction of 45%. Lower limb vascular Doppler ultrasound did not indicate deep vein thrombosis.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Progression of bilateral pulmonary lesions prompted bedside bronchoscopy, revealing diffuse mucosal hemorrhage; metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid identified Leptospira interrogans and Aspergillus flavus, confirmed by BAL fungal culture. Cessation of empiric carbapenem/glycopeptide therapy and administration of targeted intravenous penicillin G combined with voriconazole led to prompt clinical and radiological resolution.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Bronchoscopy displayed diffuse blood infiltration and mucosal swelling in the left and right bronchial lumens. The bronchial alveolar lavage fluid was sent for mNGS examination. Three days later, mNGS showed seven sequence numbers of Leptospira interrogans and 1,289,906 sequences of Aspergillus flavus. A culture of the bronchial alveolar lavage fluid revealed Aspergillus flavus: 1+. Therefore, in consideration of pulmonary hemorrhagic leptospirosis complicated with pulmonary aspergillosis, administration of vancomycin, imipenem cilastatin, and voriconazole injection was stopped, and the patient was given penicillin G (400,000 U I.V. infusion, q4h) combined with voriconazole tablets (0.2 g, p.o., q12h).

editor_comments: Distillation executed according to Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology. Admission prompt captures the clinical presentation of hemoptysis, shock, ARDS, thrombocytopenia, and CTPA findings while strictly excluding bronchoscopy, mNGS results, pathogen names, and treatment response.
